[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Jordan from Redwood, I'm joined by Maya, our platform SE. Quick audio check?
[00:15] Maya: Hey hi, good to go.
[00:18] Liam: Yep good audio, thanks.
[00:22] Jordan: Cool. High level for today we want to run through the SDK quickstart for Python and TypeScript, show auth patterns, environment setup for local and CI, and then a short console and Optimize tips section. We'll try to keep this interactive so stop us if you have questions.
[00:38] Noah: Sounds good, our main constraints are data residency and predictable 100ms-ish token latency for our chat endpoints, and we want a clear path to POC.
[00:48] Jordan: Great, noted.

[01:10] Maya: Alright I'll share my screen, starting with the SDK install. For Python we recommend pip install redwood-inference (note: transcript may mangle package name), for TypeScript npm install @redwood/inference or yarn add @redwood/inference, and there's a one-file quickstart for both.
[01:36] Sofia: Quick question — do we need special runtime or can we run from our laptop?
[01:40] Maya: You can run locally from laptop for dev, we ship a lightweight client that talks to the hosted API. For production you'd point to dedicated or private endpoints.

[02:12] Maya: Auth options — simplest is API key (per-service or per-route). For enterprise we support SSO via SAML / SCIM for user access, and service accounts with KMS-backed keys for programmatic access. There's also a rotating CI secret pattern we recommend.
[02:34] Liam: For CI secrets, how do you recommend rotation? We like short-lived tokens but need seamless rotation in pipelines.
[02:40] Jordan: Two options — short-lived service tokens via our token-exchange endpoint (issuer rotation), or use a pipeline step to fetch a key from your KMS and inject into env at runtime. We have examples in the repo.

[03:05] Maya: Let me jump to an example — Python snippet (read aloud): "from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_KEY']); resp = client.generate(... )". In TS it's similar: import { RedwoodClient } from '@redwood/inference' ... new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY }).
[03:30] Sofia: Are there per-route keys? We have different product teams and want to separate quota.
[03:34] Maya: Yes — you can create per-route API keys via Console, assign quotas and rate limits per key, and trace attribution in the Console logs.

[04:00] Noah: How about SSO for developers vs service accounts for apps — can we mix?
[04:05] Jordan: Absolutely, we recommend SSO for interactive user access and service accounts for production services. Console RBAC allows you to scope who can create keys, who can see logs, etc.

[04:35] Maya: Now the env setup. For local dev we use dotenv (.env) for secrets but we emphasize never committing .env. For CI use your secret manager (GH Secrets, GitLab, Vault) and inject at runtime. Example CI snippet we have for GitHub Actions that reads a REDWOOD_KEY from secrets and sets it in env for the step.
[05:02] Liam: Any recommended pattern for multi-env (dev/stage/prod)?
[05:06] Maya: Use separate API keys and separate projects/environments in Console. That way you can pin model versions per env and keep metrics separate.

[05:30] Jordan: Quick Console tour — Maya can show model selection and per-route config.
[05:34] Maya: (screen) On the Console you create a Route, pick a model from the catalog — we have curated open models and Redwood-verified perf profiles — then you can set batching, cache TTL for prefix caching, and attach a key. You can also set automatic fallback policies to lower-cost model variants if capacity is constrained.
[06:00] Sofia: That fallback policy is interesting — if we need consistent latency how does fallback affect that?
[06:07] Maya: Fallback is a graceful degradation — you can configure tolerances. If latency SLO is top priority, you'd route to lower-latency model variants or to Dedicated capacity. Fallback is mostly for availability and cost smoothing.

[06:35] Jordan: Now let's talk about Optimize hints — for your workload (short chat turns) you'll want to enable KV cache reuse for conversation state, set continuous batching thresholds tuned to your RPS, and consider int8 quantization if you can accept slight quality delta for a big cost win.
[06:58] Liam: We definitely want cost control obvious metrics. Does Console show per-token cost per route?
[07:03] Maya: Yes, Console has token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route and per model. You can also export usage to your billing and set alerts.

[07:30] (little cross-talk)

[07:50] Maya: I want to show a small local demo — I'll run a quick TypeScript example hitting the sandbox.
[07:56] Jordan: Note — sandbox keys are limited and aligned to the POC quota we discussed in pre-call.
[08:08] Maya: (types) Running... ok call returns, transcript: "Hello from Redwood sandbox". Sorry the sample content is tiny, but this shows the dev loop: change prompt, run, iterate.
[08:30] Sofia: Looks good. What's the SDK behavior when token limits are hit? Do we get a clear error?
[08:36] Maya: You receive a 429 with a helpful message and a retry-after. We also surface token usage in real time. For long-running responses we stream and provide partial content as available.

[09:00] Noah: For the POC we want to test private deployment — VPC or on-prem — we have to pass security review. Can you summarize differences quickly?
[09:12] Jordan: Sure — Hosted is fastest to onramp but data leaves your VPC. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools within Redwood's infra with better isolation and SLAs. Private deployment installs the control plane in your VPC (or on-prem) and supports HSM/KMS integrations, audit logs kept in your environment, and optional air-gapped packaging. Performance characteristics are similar but networking and compliance vary.
[09:45] Liam: For Private, do we manage the model files as well or do you push updates?
[09:50] Maya: Customers can choose to host model weights in their environment or let Redwood manage model artifacts with strict access controls. For sensitive workloads we often recommend customer-managed artifacts.

[10:20] Jordan: Jumping back to SDK details — error handling patterns and retries. Use idempotency keys for multi-step generate patterns, exponential backoff for transient errors, and monitor per-route latencies in Console.

[10:45] Maya: Also note the SDK supports streaming in both Python and TS — so you can wire streaming events directly to your websocket or web client.

[11:00] Liam: Any gotchas for TypeScript typing and the response schema?
[11:04] Maya: We have generated typings. The response has choices, tokens, and a usage block. Some customers parse streaming tokens differently but the SDK has helpers to reconstruct final content.

[11:30] (short pause)

[11:45] Sofia: Security question — do you keep logs of prompts/outputs by default?
[11:50] Jordan: For hosted we default to storing logs for observability but customers can opt out or set retention policies, and for Private you control log retention entirely. We can also redact sensitive fields via the Console or ingestion hooks.

[12:20] Noah: Are there SOC2/ISO artifacts we can review?
[12:24] Jordan: Yes we'll send the SOC2 summary and our security whitepaper after the call (action item).

[12:40] Maya: Ok next part, quick deep-dive on batching and cache. Batching consolidates concurrent short requests to increase GPU throughput; cache (prefix/KV) keeps conversation state local to avoid re-sending the entire history. For your chat POC we expect large savings if you enable both.
[13:10] Liam: How transparent is cache invalidation? If we change system prompts do we need to flush?
[13:16] Maya: You can set TTLs or explicit invalidation via API. We recommend versioned route keys when changing system prompts.

[13:40] Jordan: Let's talk perf targets for POC — you mentioned 100-150ms per token goal. For short-turn chat with batching disabled, on Dedicated or Private it's achievable, but on Hosted it depends on model and region. We'll include perf profiles in the docs we send.

[14:10] Sofia: For benchmarking, what should we measure?
[14:13] Maya: Measure p95 latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, and end-to-end tail latency including network. We'll provide a small benchmark harness (Python + TS) that hits routes with a reproducible prompt distribution.

[14:40] (Jordan types link into chat: link to security doc and repo — represented as note)

[15:00] Maya: Quick note about model variants — the Console lets you pin a model version for a route, and rollout to new variants via canary or A/B. Rollouts support automatic fallback to previous model if quality drops.

[15:30] Liam: For canary, do you do percentage rollouts?
[15:33] Maya: Yes you can split traffic by percentage or by header-based routing.

[15:50] Noah: We're concerned about costs during dev spikes — can we set hard caps?
[15:55] Jordan: You can set quota limits on API keys and per-project budgets and get alerts. For Dedicated we can also provision burst capacity controls.

[16:20] Sofia: For storage of embeddings, do you support vector DB integrations?
[16:25] Maya: We don't host long-term vector DBs in Console but we have connectors and integration patterns; many customers store embeddings in their own DBs. We do provide a similarity-retrieval helper in SDK.
